gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a generator charge rate. For a battery-plus-generator kit, the generator's charge rate sets refill time and fuel use. Anker's Smart Generator 5500 feeds the E10 at 4,500 W DC, so it refills a 2-battery E10 (12.288 kWh) in about 2.7 h, and Anker says one 10 L tank holds about 17 kWh, or about 1.4 refills. If you plug an existing 120 V portable generator into the E10, the E10 charges at 1,800 W or less, so the same refill takes about 7–8 h.
standout_why: I compared against the four pages ChatGPT cited (FranklinWH's 'Can I use a generator' article, both URLs; the Generator Module page; the aPower 2 page) and one it got but didn't cite ('How does aPower charge batteries by generator?'). None gives a generator charge rate in kW, a refill time, start/stop charge levels or fuel per kWh. They say only 'match rated wattage to essential loads'. ChatGPT's table (10–26 kW generators) sizes the generator to the house load. On the E10, generator watts reach the battery through a charge port: 4.5 kW DC from Anker's generator, or 1.8 kW / 7.68 kW AC from a third-party 120 V / 240 V generator. That limit decides which generator goes in the cart. A shopper's existing 120 V portable generator would take about 3× longer to refill the batteries.
kit_items: Battery + inverter: Anker SOLIX E10 Power Module + 2× B6000 (2 × 6.144 = 12.288 kWh). It runs 7,680 W continuous at 240 V, enough for the whole house through a 200 A Power Dock. Anker's 10 L ≈ 17 kWh claim means one tank is about 1.4 refills.

Automatic transfer: Anker SOLIX Power Dock (200 A service entry, switchover in 20 ms or less per Anker). Its generator circuits are rated 100 A max / 80 A continuous, so a later standby generator can be added.

Generator: Anker SOLIX Smart Generator 5500 (tri-fuel). It's the only generator here that uses the E10's 4,500 W DC generator input: 4,500 W on gasoline or LPG, 4,000 W on natural gas. It can start automatically at a battery level you set. A 120 V third-party generator would charge at 1.8 kW or less.

More storage (optional): Anker SOLIX B6000 Battery Module, +6.144 kWh, up to 5 per E10. With 3 batteries (18.432 kWh), a refill at 4.5 kW takes about 4.1 h, and one tank (≈17 kWh) no longer fills them.

findings.label: DC generator input
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX E10 – Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: Refill of 2 × B6000 from empty with no house load: 12.288 kWh ÷ 4.5 kW = 2.73 h. With 3 modules: 18.432 ÷ 4.5 = 4.1 h. The Solar Lab measured 87% efficiency, so expect somewhat longer in practice.

findings.label: AC charge input from grid or third-party generator
findings.source_title: Automatic Generator Integration for Home Battery Backup – Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: Anker: 'continuous charging above 12 A should stay under 3 hours' at 120 V. 12.288 kWh at 120 V: 3 h × 1.8 kW = 5.4 kWh, then 6.888 kWh at 1.44 kW (12 A × 120 V) = 4.8 h, about 7.8 h total (6.8 h at a flat 1.8 kW). At 240 V: 12.288 ÷ 7.68 = 1.6 h.

findings.label: AC generator bypass / Power Dock generator circuit rating
findings.value: Up to 9,600 W bypass via E10 AC Generator Adapter; Power Dock generator circuits 100 A max / 80 A continuous
findings.source_title: Automatic Generator Integration for Home Battery Backup – Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: Anker also says a third-party standby generator must be 240 V with two-wire or utility-sensing control, max surge 24 kW. While a standby generator runs, the battery does not power the home, so that generator must be sized to the household load.

findings.label: AC input limit as set in the app (measured)
findings.value: Input capped at 20 A / 4,800 W at 240 V until reconfigured; the limit is 80% of the 'Running Wattage' setting (7,200 W × 0.8 = 5,760 W)
findings.source_title: Powering your house with an EV: testing the Anker SOLIX E10 (EV Outdoors)
findings.note: Ken Yannacci (EV Outdoors, 2026-03-27) tested with a Silverado EV as the 240 V source. For a third-party 240 V generator, set Running Wattage to the generator's rating. Charge input will be 80% of that, so a 7.2 kW generator charges at 5.76 kW, not 7.68 kW.

findings.label: Idle draw and efficiency (measured)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX E10 Review: Best Whole-Home Battery Backup? – The Solar Lab
findings.note: The Solar Lab's own measurement. 40 W × 24 h = 0.96 kWh/day of overhead, about 7.8% of 12.288 kWh. Usable energy is about 12.288 × 0.87 ≈ 10.7 kWh.

findings.label: DC output to E10 / AC output
findings.value: 4,500 W DC (gasoline, LPG), 4,000 W DC (natural gas); 3,600 W AC continuous at 120 V; 5,500 W starting
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX Smart Generator 5500 – Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: On natural gas: 12.288 kWh ÷ 4.0 kW = 3.07 h refill. DC output requires the E10. The page lists auto-start by battery level.

findings.label: Fuel tank and energy per tank
findings.value: 10 L (2.64 gal) metal tank, about 17 kWh per tank (Anker claim); 224 cc engine; 69 dB(A) at 7 m in Eco mode; 110 lb
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX Smart Generator 5500 – Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: 17 kWh ÷ 12.288 kWh = 1.38 full refills of the 2-battery kit per tank. 17 kWh ÷ 4.5 kW ≈ 3.8 h at full DC output per tank. That's 1.7 kWh per liter, Anker's figure, not independently measured.
